source.title: Compute-Optimal Scaling for Value-Based Deep RL
source.authors: Preston Fu; Oleh Rybkin; Zhi-Yuan Zhou; Michal Nauman; P. Abbeel; Sergey Levine; Aviral Kumar

record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling-law analysis to online value-based deep reinforcement learning, using TD-error, data efficiency, and RL return rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The paper reports RL scaling fits and compute-allocation results, not language-model loss results. Its results concern data required to reach an RL return threshold and allocations between model size and UTD ratio. Cited language-model scaling results and prior-work results borrowed for comparison are not recorded as this study's findings.
record.test_reason: It fits power-law data-efficiency and compute-allocation laws for online value-based deep RL, a new training regime, and reports their fit and extrapolation errors. That bears on V5. It measures no language-model loss, so V1–V4, V6 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly right. The authors claim to have established scaling laws for value-based RL: batch size, data efficiency, and data/compute versus budget are predictable, with extrapolation errors around 18%. They identify TD-overfitting as the reason larger models tolerate larger batches. They also note that the optimal UTD/model-size split is task-dependent, sometimes unpredictable, and has broad near-optimal regions.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits RL data efficiency and RL compute allocation for value-based TD learning, rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy against parameters, tokens, and training compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Task/domain, batch-size selection, UTD ratio, model size, and fitting procedure affect the reported RL scaling results. Borrowed fixed-batch data could produce unstable fits; the authors use shared exponents or task aggregation in response.

fits_no_version.finding: The best batch size grows with model size and falls with UTD ratio, following a fitted rational/power form. Its relative error is 48.9%, versus 55.1% for a log-linear fit.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In TD learning, the maximal admissible batch size grows with model capacity (TD-overfitting), unlike in supervised learning.

record.problems: The evidence concerns simulated RL tasks and RL return/data-efficiency measures, not language-model cross-entropy. Full three-dimensional batch-size sweeps were run on 4 tasks; results for 13 DMC tasks were borrowed from prior work with a constant batch size that the authors say did not always represent best achievable data efficiency. Some allocation trends are described as unpredictable, and the authors note that several hyperparameter settings can perform similarly.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable. The record includes the directly relevant data-efficiency and compute-allocation findings; it omits unrelated TD-error, passive-critic, learning-rate, and target-update-rate experiments.

untested.parts: All. No language-model held-out loss is measured.
Language-model loss extrapolation. Only RL data-efficiency extrapolation is tested.
Parameter/token allocation for language models. The RL UTD/model-size allocation is recorded under V5.
All. Only width is varied, and parameter count is not held fixed.
Image, video and other modalities; repeated data; fine-tuning and transfer.
Dependence of language-model exponents on parameter counting, schedule, data or fitting method. Disagreement among published laws.

missing.what: Optimal data and compute versus budget F fit as power laws. R² is about 0.99 for most tasks, but h1-pole compute is 0.34 and h1-stand is 0.68/0.87.
Optimal UTD and model size versus budget. h1-pole R² is -0.06 (UTD) and 0.32 (model size); humanoid-stand R² is 0.94 for both.
Compute-optimal allocation versus σ-only scaling (1.26× data) and N-only scaling (1.11× data).

record.verdict_notes: Every result concerns small RL critic networks (up to about 36M parameters) on simulated control tasks, with sample efficiency to a return threshold as the outcome rather than loss. The study is therefore only a V5 regime-extension test. The reader's V7 links were removed because V7 concerns published language-model scaling laws. The TD-error and learning-rate experiments do not bear on any version.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether small language-model runs predict much larger language-model losses. The paper evaluates extrapolation of RL data efficiency instead.
The stated parameter-count and token-count allocation laws for language-model compute budgets. The paper allocates RL compute between model size and UTD ratio.

Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details on language-model loss at fixed parameter count. The paper varies width for RL models and does not hold parameter count fixed while testing architecture shape.

Other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer, and the claimed language-model held-out loss measure. This study tests power-law scaling in online value-based RL using RL data efficiency and compute allocation.
Predictability of language-model downstream task performance from scale or pretraining loss.

Whether language-model exponents and compute-optimal parameter/token splits depend on language-model counting, schedules, data, or fitting choices. The paper reports task- and fitting-related variation in RL scaling.
